profiles.name: Alabama
profiles.imageReviewBasis: Existing inspected image identification/rights/scope record; no new image pixels or clearance invented.
remainingGaps: Compare early southeastern history, separate family migrations and East Texas land negotiations with original records and specialist scholarship. Compressed accounts and Martin’s related publications are not independent corroborations; the 1836/1839 instruments and the 1954 implementation proclamation remain to inspect.

Resolve what separate event or instrument may explain the Oklahoma community history’s April 1939 statement. The historical constitution records Interior approval in November 1938 and ratification in January 1939; these dates are kept distinct.

Review later constitutional amendments, ordinances and implementation before describing present governing or citizenship rules. No current officeholders, enrollment totals, territorial boundary or individual legal rights are determined here.

Expand community voices and publicly shared cultural life, including artists, foodways, land use, families and Oklahoma perspectives. A named educator and one student interview are valuable particular accounts, not a complete account of everyone’s experience. Community review has not been recorded.

Establish current teaching access, learner experiences and outcomes through suitable community evidence. No speaker census or independent pronunciation/audio evaluation is supplied; older language studies remain further-reading leads where full content access was limited.
Follow the 2025 transportation final draft through adoption, funding and implementation records. Its schedule and goals are not completed improvements or current verified safety rates.

Recheck current website editorial provenance and dated institutional information. The earlier aqtt.org page is excluded as current community authority pending verification; this does not establish fraud, compromise or a reconstruction. Linked institutional records support the replacement historical publication’s attribution, not the currency of every assertion.

Confirm rights and appropriate community context before later image reuse or mapping. Broad state associations are evidence notes, not homeland polygons, sensitive-site locations or an exhaustive regional directory.
Earlier records, migration/land instruments and conflicting Oklahoma chronology need closer comparison.
Broader community voices, present learning outcomes and later government/planning implementation remain open.
The Oklahoma community account’s April 1939 statement remains distinct from the constitution’s November 1938 approval and January 1939 ratification.
Dictionary inspection covered specified grammar, handout and entry samples, not the entire 1993 book or audio; present learning outcomes remain unverified.

Expand current Coushatta-authored historical and institutional accounts without treating Texas, Louisiana and Oklahoma communities as interchangeable.
Inspect the 1954 proclamation, relevant state records and original treaty/ratification documents where accessible; keep statutory text distinct from later implementation.
Resolve contradictions in chief dates and organizational chronology through further evidence; do not silently choose whichever source sounds convenient.
Restore legitimate archive access if available later, with collection-level cultural permissions respected; no contact or restricted-material access attempted.
No present population, language vitality census, private genealogy or program outcome has been established.

The selected2025 Texas higher-education packet is an administrative publication, not a study of student experiences, awards or outcomes. Current program operation and other Coushatta governments require separate review.
The Texas statute’s contemplated proclamation and its implementation record were not inspected; later legal interpretation remains outside scope.
The treaty is an edited transcription; manuscript, ratification record and Indigenous responses were not examined here.
The 1932 secondary article is dated and draws on older terminology and sources; further Coushatta-authored history and direct archival research would improve the account.
The digital dictionary was sampled through four entries; full vocabulary coverage, grammar, additional teaching materials and present-day language context remain open.
Current community conditions and each Texas, Louisiana and Oklahoma government’s own contemporary publications require further review; no present census or language-use estimate is claimed.
No community review or endorsement has been recorded.
Community histories remain attributed syntheses; underlying instruments and conflicting chief/organizational dates need further review.
No present speaker census, current program guarantee or identical language practice across communities is established.

profiles.name: Caddo

The three historical confederacies and named local communities are not fully surveyed here; terms vary across oral history, colonial records, and later scholarship.
The 1835 treaty is read as a printed statutory text only; signed manuscript, ratification files, later agreements, and implementation records were not separately inspected.

Archaeological interpretations of ancestral continuity and the northern Arkansas Basin remain debated; no fixed homeland boundary is asserted.
No present population figure, current fluent-speaker count, exhaustive community list, or claim of community endorsement is made.

Post-removal history, constituent historical communities and the debated northern Arkansas Basin affiliation need deeper community-centered comparison.
The constitutional-project page describes consultation and planned drafting, not adopted changes; the inaccessible journal remains an unread lead.

profiles.name: Coahuiltecan

The origin and scope of the term “Coahuiltecan” conflict across sources: the 2014 CHAPS chapter describes later scholarly usage while the current NPS visitor page attributes it to Spanish geography. The reviewed material does not settle this disagreement.
Mission registers and language records are incomplete; group-to-language and group-to-place identifications require more primary-source and specialist review.

No community review or endorsement is recorded. Tāp Pīlam Coahuiltecan Nation and Miakan/Garza Band / Indigenous Cultures Institute are distinct sources and should not be treated as interchangeable or exhaustive.
The Institute language page contains an internally inconsistent speaker-status statement; no current speaker count or language-vitality conclusion is made.
The 2001 NPS report and 1985 mission study are dated. Their consultation recommendations and legal discussion do not establish current status.

Selected methodological and final-comment pages of the INAH language-history article have now been inspected. Its vocabulary tables and cited originals remain unevaluated, its broad disappearance assertions are not adopted, and its publication dates conflict internally. More focused community-directed and specialist language evidence remains needed.
No current population, exhaustive descendant list, legal recognition status, or specific map association is asserted.
Sources disagree about the term’s origin; the selected material does not settle the disagreement or demonstrate all deep-time continuity claims.
The 1985 mission study is dated and partially inspected; language-to-group identifications, original registers and current legal status remain outside this guide.

The collection has twelve substantive works, but many analyze the same uneven Spanish documentary record; source quantity does not resolve the historical identity debate.
The 1986 Kelley monograph and 1988 Hickerson linguistic article remain partially inspected or abstract-only; the full texts were not reviewed.
Spanish and Mexican archival manuscripts discussed in the secondary literature, including the 1683–84 Domínguez de Mendoza diary, were not independently read.
The range of contemporary Jumano community publications, family histories, language evidence, and cultural transmission remains limited and needs further review.

The relationships among historical Jumano labels, Taovayas/Wichita, Tompiro Pueblo communities, and La Junta peoples remain contested; no exhaustive descent, identity, population, or federal recognition claim is made.
Historical maps described or reproduced in secondary pages were not independently inspected for this batch; no map-to-profile connection was added.
The August and October 1683 Arizona Historical Indexes records are metadata-only leads; read the cited archival documents and translations before using their catalogue summaries as evidence.
The new article's manuscript comparisons and historical conclusions were read as published scholarship; no underlying archival text was independently checked.
The encyclopedia’s disappearance wording is a dated documentary interpretation, not evidence that descendants disappeared; colonial manuscripts remain unreviewed.
The translation article’s extracted publisher text was inspected previously, but a later download recheck failed; no fresh availability or page-image review is claimed.

profiles.name: Atakapa
profiles.imageReviewBasis: Existing inspected image identification/rights/scope record; no new image pixels or clearance invented.
remainingGaps: The colonial and early ethnographic record needs closer review in French, Spanish and original archival materials; broad labels such as Atakapa, Akokisa and Deadose are not always used consistently.

The language guide relies on historical documentation alongside a collaborative online resource. The full Kimball grammar was not accessed, and present learning activity or outcomes should not be inferred from resource availability.
Archaeological, regional oral-history and mission histories need deeper comparison. No historical map was added because a sourced map/community connection was not reviewed in this batch.

A Louisiana Attakapas Eagle Band webpage now supplies that group’s self-description, but the relation between the Band’s longer Four Winds affiliation name and the Governor’s roster label “Four Winds Cherokee,” and the Band’s state-recognition claim, remain unresolved from these short records. Additional relevant community and government documentation would be needed.

Perspectives from other organized groups and descendant communities remain uneven; the Louisiana Attakapas Eagle Band is represented only by its short self-description and a public state roster whose wording does not settle the organization’s relationship to the listed Four Winds Cherokee entry.

The 2021 Texas Observer interview supplies an important but individually scoped Akokisa perspective. Independent archaeological and archival corroboration is still needed for historical-site and deep-time statements; sensitive places should not be republished.
Original Spanish/French records, mission files, specialist archaeology and the Smithsonian’s Swanton/Morse manuscript cards remain unread.
Current community perspectives are meaningful but not comprehensive across all groups connected to the historical label.
The complete Kimball grammar and Darensbourg–Kaufman language-renewal chapter were not accessed.
No community review is recorded; historical identity and group relationships remain unresolved in the sources examined.

The 2021 Texas Observer interview is one elder’s reported perspective; its accompanying map and underlying archaeological evidence were not independently reviewed, and sensitive cultural-site details are deliberately omitted.
Historical group relations and colonial accounts need further comparison; no single present recognition, genealogy or disappearance claim follows from the collection.
Dictionary inspection sampled entries and visible summaries; the full dynamic grammar and audio were not reviewed, and contents are linked without copying.

profiles.name: Karankawa
profiles.imageReviewBasis: Existing inspected image identification/rights/scope record; no new image pixels or clearance invented.
remainingGaps: The complete text of the replacement marker announced in July 2026 was not verified in an updated official Texas Historical Commission record.

The 2023 Karankawa Kadla and 2026 Karankawa Tribe of Texas publications use different names; their precise organizational relationship and the breadth of each community’s representation were not independently established.
The selected 2022 commission packet pages contain proposed motions and submitted material; the final action on that agenda item was not established from minutes.
Primary Spanish, Mexican and Republic-era records and archaeological publications require further source-by-source inspection; TSHA and Texas Beyond History bibliographies remain leads.
The full 2019 honors thesis was not read cover to cover; the full text of the 2021 peer-reviewed war article remains unread and excluded.
Further descendant-led publications and perspectives should be reviewed without assuming one organization speaks for all Karankawa descendants.
No current population estimate, exhaustive list of contemporary organizations, or legal-recognition status claim is made; no community endorsement or review is recorded.
No new historical-map association was added: this source batch did not inspect a specific archival map and its relevance to an individual community.
Older extinction-era historical framing must remain attributed and cannot negate living descendants; cited colonial originals remain unreviewed.
The relationship among dated Karankawa Kadla/Five Rivers Council/Karankawa Tribe of Texas labels and the full replacement-marker wording remain unresolved.

profiles.name: Tonkawa
profiles.imageReviewBasis: Existing inspected image identification/rights/scope record; no new image pixels or clearance invented.
remainingGaps: The 1862 massacre article is a secondary interpretation; seek further public Tonkawa-authored or community-held accounts and compare more of the original government records. Do not force a single-cause explanation from the present evidence.
The timing/direction of earlier movement, composition of named bands, language classification, and archaeological associations remain contested or uncertain.

The 1837 treaty, 1891 agreement, and 1907 memorial have been read, but related federal/Republic records, ratification/implementation documentation, and later claim disposition still require systematic review.

The 1846 Council Springs treaty text and signatory pages have been inspected, but its separate 1847 advice-and-consent and presidential ratification instruments, implementation record, and Tonkawa-specific interpretations remain unread.

Current community-authored cultural, language-program, and historical publications need broader review. The 2020 museum booklet and large dictionary were not fully inspected; failed automated access is not treated as a paywall.
The documentary site describes collaboration and an oral-history film project, but neither film nor interviews were viewed; culturally sensitive footage may require limits on public use.
Current population, enrollment, acreage, and program-status figures are not claimed from undated pages.
This review did not inspect or add maps.

The 1996 Fifth Circuit opinion resolves a narrow dispute over the Texas 1866 act on the record before that court; its underlying legislative/administrative materials and later treatment have not been surveyed. Do not extend its holding to broader Tonkawa homeland history or current identity.

The 1862 massacre article is a secondary interpretation. Tonkawa-authored or community-held public accounts of the event and the original underlying government records need further review; no single-cause explanation is adopted.
The 1846 Council Springs treaty scan’s transcribed text and signatory pages were read; separate ratification instruments, later implementation, and Tonkawa-specific interpretations remain unreviewed.

The 1996 appellate decision addresses a specific claim under the 1866 Texas act; the underlying legislative record and later case treatment were not reviewed, and the ruling is not extended to broad homeland or present-identity questions.
Read the memorial against the contrasting federal cession account already catalogued as p394-s10; neither alone establishes shared consent, implementation or valuation.
The dictionary, film and audio remain unread; the powwow page contains its own restriction language and is excluded from this starter path.

profiles.name: Lipan Apache
profiles.imageReviewBasis: Existing inspected image identification/rights/scope record; no new image pixels or clearance invented.
remainingGaps: The 1838 and 1844 treaty scans linked by the Tribe were not readable in the available reader; do not treat the landing pages as inspected treaty text. The 1846 multination treaty was read, but its implementation and Lipan-specific response remain unverified.
The 2026 UTEP dissertation and 2016 UTRGV thesis were inspected only through repository abstracts; full texts returned automated HTTP 403 responses and remain unread and uncounted.
The TSHA article is an outside historical synthesis; its bibliography points to community historians, archival records and scholarship that require separate review.
The 1903/1904 difference for Lipan arrivals at the Mescalero community and the 1934/1936 reorganization dates need source-level resolution.
The Texas State Library and Archives map 01413 remains metadata-only; the image was not inspected and no map-to-profile association has been made.

The Webster place-name article is based primarily on one narrator’s 1938 account and includes unidentified locations; it cannot support a fixed homeland boundary or broad conclusions about all Lipan place-naming practices.
Current legal status, enrollment, population, language use and relationships among Lipan communities in Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma and northern Mexico require further, carefully scoped research.
No community review or endorsement has been recorded.

The 1838 and 1844 treaty scans linked by the Tribe were not readable in the available reader; do not treat the landing pages as inspected treaty text. The 1846 multination treaty was read, but it does not establish implementation or a uniform Lipan response.

The Webster place-name article is based primarily on one narrator’s 1938 account, includes some unidentified locations, and should not be used to draw a fixed homeland boundary or generalize beyond its own small sample.

The 1876 Fort Griffin report is a federal administrative compilation. Its statements concern one Lipan group and federal policy; underlying records, a Lipan-authored interpretation, and whether recommendations were implemented remain unverified.

The 2024 Marfa Public Radio report is a useful dated local case study, not a comprehensive history written by the Tribe; the audio was not played, and its accounts should remain attributed to the interviewees.
Lipan/Mescalero arrival and reorganization dates remain inconsistent across accounts; original records and broader community voices still need comparison.
Full dissertation/thesis texts and the 1838/1844 treaty scans remain unread leads; proposed federal legislation is not enacted status.

profiles.name: Mescalero Apache
profiles.imageReviewBasis: Existing inspected image identification/rights/scope record; no new image pixels or clearance invented.
remainingGaps: The Tribe’s Our Culture page is undated and contains broad older language; only identity, broad geography, reservation history, and non-sensitive public foodways context were used.
The 2023 tribal commemoration says Lipan members joined the reservation community in 1905; the Tribe’s undated Our Culture page says about 1903. This difference remains unresolved.
The posted constitution is amended through October 18, 1988; newer ordinances and current legal updates were not reviewed.

TxDOT’s 2020 report was inspected selectively, not cover to cover. It is a government synthesis, though its introduction documents source approval and draft comments from the Tribe’s Historic Preservation Officer. Most cited underlying records were not independently inspected.

The NPS page gives a short historical interpretation without showing its underlying sources; its language about disappearance from the Trans-Pecos is not used to imply the disappearance of Mescalero people.

Further community-authored publications and distinct perspectives from Mescalero, Lipan, and Chiricahua members and institutions are needed. No community review or endorsement of this Atlas profile is recorded.
TxDOT report maps and figures were not visually inspected or connected to a profile; the report’s page 50 culturally sensitive planning section was deliberately not opened.
No current population, enrollment, acreage, language-program status, or other changeable figures are claimed.

The 2017 participatory-research article documents a Tribe-requested pilot and includes a broad historical homeland summary, but its cited historical sources were not independently reviewed and it does not establish current family-program availability or outcomes.
The Ndé Bizaa’ language-program page is undated and does not provide current implementation, fluency data, curriculum materials, or outcome measures.
The September 2024 language-program update is a dated snapshot: planned class start dates and recruitment are not verified as later implementation, and no follow-up outcomes were reviewed.

The 2017 participatory-research article concerns a small 2013–2014 pilot with incomplete follow-up; it does not establish current services, community-wide outcomes, or long-term effects. Its broader homeland description is not a boundary survey.

The undated Ndé Bizaa’ page states language-program goals and planned approaches but gives no current schedule, baseline, fluency counts, or measured outcomes; possible future strategies are not treated as implemented policies.
The Tribe’s pages give about 1903 and 1905 for Lipan arrivals; neither date is silently reconciled.
The report is partially inspected and remains government-authored; the small 2013–2014 pilot does not establish present availability, long-term outcomes or conditions for all families.

remainingGaps: The 1867 No-ko-aht account was recorded in shorthand by federal agent Franklin G. Adams and edited by George A. Root in 1932. The editorial narrative and attributed account differ on dates and group counts; neither is treated as independently conclusive.

Review the full 2025 TAMIU thesis; only its abstract and repository record were inspected, and the automated download returned 403 without establishing a reader access requirement.

Add distinct community perspectives from Kickapoo communities in Oklahoma, Kansas, and Mexico; this supplement cannot stand for them.

No community review or endorsement is recorded.

The UT Austin Latorre finding aid points to potentially relevant archival materials about El Nacimiento, but the collection itself was not inspected; its stated photography and image-publication restrictions must be respected.

Mager’s 2017 comparison was read only in selected sections. It shares an author with the 2010 and 2020 works, uses earlier interviews/documentary research, advances an interpretive thesis, and includes cultural descriptions outside the scope used here; its repeated claims are not independent evidence.
The 2025 transportation plan’s appendices, detailed crash data and web GIS remain unreviewed; proposed safety strategies are not treated as completed actions.
The public Chapter 20 code copy has an unverified enactment/amendment history and current status; further legal-history work is needed before describing it as current law.
The 2025 transportation plan records dated planning priorities and proposals; implementation/outcomes were not checked, and the detailed crash-data appendices and web GIS remain unreviewed.
The publicly posted Chapter 20 child-welfare code was read only in selected sections; enactment/amendment history and current consolidated status were not verified.
Wider community voices and original-record comparison remain uneven; Mager's related works are not independent corroboration.

Art-group membership is introduced, but artist biographies, dates, community meanings and image rights require more work. No artwork reproduction right follows from a linked essay.

Private family documents, raw interviews and restricted underlying materials were not accessed. Published culturally governed stories, songs and sensitive-place details were excluded from the synthesis and were not reproduced.
The nine-work collection remains uneven across historical periods and community perspectives. No community review, endorsement, comprehensive coverage or research completion is claimed.
Original 1865 negotiations, translation, implementation and subsequent land changes remain unreviewed; the edited terms are not a present legal determination.
The Palo Duro account concerns a dated commemoration and institutional memory. Original Kiowa accounts, military/civilian records and detailed battle chronology still need comparison.

Later economic and land-tenure analysis is locally scoped. No universal Kiowa percentage, individual parcel identification, current title or legal-status assessment is made.
Early movement dates conflict; original historical accounts, family histories and fuller land-tenure work remain needed.

The program reports establish stated activities rather than tested fluency or participation outcomes.

profiles.name: Shoshone
profiles.imageReviewBasis: Existing inspected image identification/rights/scope record; no new image pixels or clearance invented.
remainingGaps: The entry’s broad “Shoshone” access point cannot stand in for separate studies of the many Shoshone governments, communities, bands, and family histories. The current sample is uneven across Fort Hall, Duck Valley, Wind River, the Northwestern Band, and other Shoshone communities.

More community-authored histories, language materials, and contemporary accounts from Shoshone governments in Nevada, Utah, Idaho, and Wyoming remain to be inspected; no single source represents all communities.

The Fort Bridger Treaty text, the Shoshone-Bannock Treaty Day account, and WyoHistory describe the separate Bannock reservation and later move using different chronology. The relationship between reservation promises, relocation, and later Fort Hall governance needs further original-record review.

Mae Parry’s 2000 chapter was reviewed at selected pages only. Its family and oral-history evidence is attributed, while its historical interpretations are not treated as universal community consensus.

The Shoshone-Paiute cultural page and Eastern Shoshone About page contain undated or broad totals and historical claims that require independent checking; no current population, acreage, or deep-time claim is reused.

The Shoshone-Bannock and Shoshone-Paiute language evidence here is introductory. Comparative specialist work on Shoshone varieties, Bannock, and Northern Paiute, with each community’s terminology and stewardship preferences, remains needed.
No community review or endorsement is recorded. No historical map was independently inspected for this batch and none has been newly assigned.
More Nevada, Utah, Idaho and Wyoming community histories, specialist language work and original treaty/claims records remain needed; relocation dates differ among retained sources.
The archival photograph is catalogued only as Shoshone; individual names, exact location and band or government identity are unestablished.

profiles.name: Bannock
profiles.imageReviewBasis: Existing inspected image identification/rights/scope record; no new image pixels or clearance invented.
remainingGaps: Add more Bannock-authored or community-approved family histories and public oral histories, including experiences beyond Fort Hall; one narrator cannot represent every band or family.
Deepen the 1878 war account with community interpretation and critically assessed archival records, including differing experiences among Bannock, Northern Paiute, and Shoshone families.

Compare the published treaty text with manuscript and official publication records, and document the chronology of Fort Hall boundary changes without collapsing promises, executive orders, and later legislation into one event.
Add a dated community account of Bannock language learning and teaching outcomes; no current speaker total is asserted here.
Expand evidence on schooling, livelihoods, art, and family life, and verify permissions and cultural suitability before reproducing archival images or knowledge.
Fuller Bannock-authored family histories, 1878 conflict perspectives and original treaty/implementation records remain needed.
The treaty reproduction's Kansas/Camas Prairie difference and ratification/proclamation chronology require primary-record comparison; neither is silently corrected here.
The salmon-skin bag is catalogued jointly as Bannock-Shoshone with an unrecorded maker; preserve that exact scope and do not infer design meanings or exclusive Bannock attribution.

profiles.name: Kootenai (Ktunaxa)
profiles.imageReviewBasis: Existing inspected image identification/rights/scope record; no new image pixels or clearance invented.
remainingGaps: Further Idaho-community oral-history/public interview perspectives, and original historical records, would broaden the institutional accounts without substituting a colonial author's voice for the Tribe's own.
Separate substantive Ksanka/Kootenai community sources in Montana remain a priority; Salish and Upper Pend d'Oreille people are not interchangeable with Kootenai people within CSKT.
The Canadian Council report and map are situated institutional perspectives, not exhaustive research into each member Nation, boundary, title claim or land declaration.
An actual specialist language-learning publication and dated evaluation would strengthen the public program descriptions. No current speaker census or tested fluency outcome was established.

The Kootenai Tribe’s 2009 restoration master plan, complete technical methods/results, data release and other monitoring studies remain to be read. The 2025 USGS report is a bounded assessment of one reach and selected river-habitat indicators; it does not establish overall ecological recovery.
Independent Montana-community perspectives are limited to explicit peer identification in these sources.
The Canadian Council’s work is not a substitute for the four member First Nations’ own detailed histories.
The 2003 hearing is a dated coalition policy statement, not a full Kootenai history; the 2025 USGS study covers one restoration reach and selected physical indicators.
Current law, broader program outcomes and quantitative language conditions remain outside the review.
Montana Ksanka and separate Canadian member-Nation histories, public oral histories and specialist language evidence remain underrepresented.
No current speaker census, legal boundary, full treaty determination or overall ecological recovery follows from these institutional accounts.
The image depicts public-refuge wetlands near Bonners Ferry; it is regional environmental context, not tribal members, reservation land or all Ktunaxa communities.

profiles.name: Coeur d'Alene
profiles.imageReviewBasis: Existing inspected image identification/rights/scope record; no new image pixels or clearance invented.
remainingGaps: The Tribe’s history, history-page acreage descriptions and older legal records need fuller comparison with community-authored histories and archival records.
Archaeology, family histories, foodways, arts, and community perspectives beyond the selected public materials remain underrepresented.
The 1995 EIS contains sensitive cultural-resource detail and dated governmental framing; the public summary omits locations and should not be treated as a full account.
Current constitutional and governmental details should be verified against current Tribe publications before being stated as current.
Environmental cleanup figures and schedules change; this guide preserves a 2024 bulletin as a dated snapshot and EPA’s live status as reviewed October 23, 2026.
Family histories, archaeology, arts and foodways remain thin, and early land/governance accounts still require comparative work.
The 1947 constitution and dated agreements cannot establish present rules; cleanup figures and status require their retained review dates.

Seltice's image is a photograph of an 1891 outside sculptor's bronze relief; retain the museum's colonial classification context rather than calling it a photograph of the living sitter or Tribe-made art.
